catalog_quote: [1991 p.51, sec. 2.1 Stress] Stress placement is very regular in Tomini-Tolitoli languages and thus empirically defines the domain of (word) phonology. It falls on the penultimate syllable of a (phonological) word and 'remains' penultimate when suffixes or clitics are added. Examples: 1a) bá'i 'head' b) ba'inye 'his/her head' Exceptions to this rule are very few in number and are dealt with in the following sections. [p.51, sec. 2.2 Paragogic vowel] In Lauje, the single most pervasive exception to the stress rule described above is the possible addition of a mid front vowel (/e/) to all consonant final words. Stress does not move to the penultimate syllable, it remains rather on the antepenultima: 2) lábong/lábonge 'house' [p.63, sec. 4] All Tomini-Tolitoli languages investigated so far share the basic phonological characteristics dealt with in the preceding sections: they show regular penultimate stress (2.1); ... [table headed Lauje Tialo Dondo Dampelas Boano Totoli; row 'paragogic vowel': Dondo +] [2001 p.73, sec. 3.4.8 Stress] Stress is usually not indicated, since it regularly falls on the penultimate syllable in all Tomini-Tolitoli languages. Only the exceptions to this rule are marked. ... Most exceptions to the general stress rule are well-motivated (either a phonetically long vowel is shortened (cf. §3.4.6 above) or stress moves to the first member of a sequence of unlike vowels as in taipang 'mango', which occurs as an alternate to the regular taipang).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word; suffixes shift it rightward so it stays penultimate. A paragogic vowel -E optionally added to consonant-final words (present in Dondo) is invisible to stress, so such forms surface with antepenultimate stress (lábong ~ lábongE).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No rhythmic secondary stress described. Himmelmann 2001 (PL-511 sec. 3.4.8, 3.5.10) uses 'secondary stress' (grave accent) only for the lengthening/prominence of the reduplicated syllable in accented CV-reduplication.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) paragogic /e/ (<E>) on consonant-final words does not count: stress stays on the stem penult = surface antepenult (1991 sec. 2.2; 2001 sec. 3.4.7, Dondo included, paragoge not obligatory in Dondo); (ii) word-final sequences of two identical vowels carry stress (regular if analysed as VV: metataá 'laugh'); (iii) fewer than ten items with antepenultimate stress on a non-high+high vowel sequence, often varying with the regular pattern (táipang ~ taípang 'mango'); (iv) Lauje-only: dropped final vowel of suffix/clitic leaves stress on the new ultima; (v) 2001 sec. 3.8: clitics and free possessive forms, unlike suffixes, do not shift stress. Balaesang final-closed-syllable stress (2001) does not concern Dondo.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stem + suffixes); Himmelmann 1991 states stress 'remains' penultimate when suffixes or clitics are added, while Himmelmann 2001 sec. 3.8 refines this: suffixes trigger the shift, clitics/free forms do not. Data are elicited word lists (c. 1200 items per language) recorded in isolation, i.e. citation forms, where the paragogic vowel is frequent for West Coast Lauje, Dondo and Tialo speakers (1991 p.64).
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources are Himmelmann's first-hand fieldwork descriptions of the whole Tomini-Tolitoli group (detailed statements for Lauje and Totoli); Dondo (siglum DON) is one of the languages he investigated and is named explicitly in the 1991 sec. 4 summary table and treated throughout the 2001 Sourcebook (classified there as Northern Tomini with Lauje, Tialo, Ampibabo-Lauje, p.20). No Dondo-specific deviation from the penultimate rule is reported; the only Dondo-relevant wrinkle is that Dondo has the (non-obligatory) paragogic vowel -E, which does not count for stress.
